title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
abstract: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select? (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data? Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time. Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them. These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. PODCAST SERIES AI Testing and Evaluation: Learnings from Science and Industry Discover how Microsoft is learning from other domains to advance evaluation and testing as a pillar of AI governance. Listen now Opens in a new tab Flint-interactive Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications. title: Better speech synthesis for audiobooks
abstract: Text-to-speech systems — which convert written text into synthetic speech — display impressive naturalness in applications such as chatbots and virtual assistants, where interactions last seconds. But they tend not to fare as well with longer-form content. When applied to audiobooks, for instance, conventional text-to-speech (TTS) models fail to reliably change speaking style between characters, as a human narrator would. This creates two problems for listeners: (1) distinguishing narration from dialogue and (2) identifying which character speaks which lines. To address this problem, the Audible technology team is using controllable TTS, meaning the ability to control dialogue delivery with natural-language speech descriptions (e.g., "speak in an enthusiastic, high-pitched voice"). This allows the TTS model to leverage the deep textual understanding of large language models (LLMs) to synthesize high-quality speech. Our approach involves three key innovations. First, we developed a novel data synthesis pipeline to produce speech data captioned with high-quality descriptions of speech characteristics. Training on this data enables our model to understand captions and produce audio consistent with them at inference time. Second, we created a system that automatically profiles characters in books and identifies their dialogue with 97% accuracy. It also provides captions for that dialogue, which act as stage directions for the model. Third, we used the first two techniques to synthesize audiobooks featuring distinct character voices, improving dialogue differentiation by 3.7 points on a MUSHRA (multiple stimuli with hidden reference and anchor) test, a standardized method where listeners rate audio quality on a scale from 0 to 100. Across tests in both English and Spanish, we observe statistically significant improvement in listening experience for eight out of ten voices. TTS for audiobooks Subtle defects in synthetic speech, such as unnatural prosody or monotone delivery, are tolerable for short stretches but become increasingly grating over time — and audiobook listeners engage with the same voice for 10 to 15 hours per book. This is why off-the-shelf TTS models often fail to produce enjoyable, natural audiobook narrations. Furthermore, general-purpose TTS models are designed to process individual utterances with minimal context. That’s a reasonable approach when responding to questions like "What's the weather today?", but it’s inadequate for audiobooks, where narrative coherence depends on understanding the surrounding story context. A TTS model reading dialogue needs to know whether the speaker is the protagonist confronting an antagonist or a minor character making small talk, information that may only be available in earlier chapters. Finally, general-purpose models struggle to produce character voices in a consistent and natural way across the span of an entire book, often voicing a character in a markedly different way in chapter 1 than in chapter 10. Controllable text-to-speech I. The data synthesis pipeline Whereas conventional TTS models are trained on text-speech pairs, a controllable-TTS model also requires annotations that describe how the speech sounds. The speech in the training set also needs to be highly expressive, covering the wide variety of dimensions — pitch, speaking rate, character voices, emotions, speaking styles, etc. — the model must control. Previous TTS models couldn't handle that kind of expressivity, so most existing training data is neutral in tone. We expanded the training sets through two approaches: new recordings and human captioning of existing audio data. While there are some datasets that include descriptions of prosodic features, each has its own description format: some are long, some are short, and some use single tags. title: The science behind TorchNeuron, Amazon’s new PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium chips
abstract: PyTorch is the one framework that most AI developers use to build their models. It’s a Python library of operations performed on tensors, higher-dimensional analogues of a matrix, or 2-D grid of numbers. Almost all of the crucial features of contemporary AI models, such as input data, model weights, and attention mechanisms, are represented by tensors, and PyTorch drastically simplifies writing code to manipulate them. This week, we announced the availability of TorchNeuron, an open-source backend that translates PyTorch code into operations executable on AWS Trainium systems. PyTorch code that already runs on other accelerators will run on Trainium with minimal or no code changes. TorchNeuron bridges PyTorch and Trainium, and both sides gain from it. PyTorch developers can now run their code on Trainium, which was built from the ground up for large-tensor workloads. They can also tap the AWS Neuron SDK, which includes a profiler that traces each instruction with cycle-level accuracy and the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI, pronounced "Nikki"), which enables control almost at the assembly level. TorchNeuron includes several optimizations that enable PyTorch code to run efficiently on Trainium, including caching at multiple levels and an optional “adaptive eager” mode that doesn’t execute individual operations one by one, as is typical in plain eager mode, but instead groups and compiles operations for more efficient execution, approaching fully compiled performance. Much of the innovation behind TorchNeuron, however, is the way its performance was evaluated. AI agents searched through hundreds of thousands of open-source models and categorized them according to their architectural characteristics. This allowed the Annapurna team around Khaled ElGalaind and Sarang Ozarde to identify 841 representative models covering the full spectrum of model architectures. From those models, they also distilled tens of thousands of practically important tensor dimensions, or “shapes”, which were then used to tune and benchmark TorchNeuron’s performance. The result is that PyTorch programmers can trust TorchNeuron to execute their code accurately, efficiently, and most importantly, right out of the box. Runtime optimizations Adaptive eager mode Standard PyTorch has two native execution modes. One is called “eager”, meaning that PyTorch operations are executed immediately, in program order. The other mode is compiled mode, where the programmer selects blocks of code that should be compiled in the traditional sense, meaning that a compiler builds a control-flow graph of the tensor operations and optimizes it. There are many optimization techniques in place today, such as operator fusion to reduce memory traffic and increase locality. Developers often use eager mode when they’re debugging models and compiled mode once they’re confident their code is correct and want it to execute as efficiently as possible. TorchNeuron adds something in-between, an opt-in setting called adaptive eager mode, which offers some of the advantages of compilation but operates on smaller subgraphs. This mode approximates both eager mode’s responsiveness and compiled mode’s performance. At run time, a Python interpreter running on a CPU accumulates instructions it gets from PyTorch ’s operator dispatch and builds small graphs. The graphs are sent to TorchNeuron, which compiles them, caches them, and puts them in a queue for execution. Multiple such graph collections and compilations are happening in parallel, further minimizing the compile time overhead. A key innovation here is that the accumulated graphs, their individual operations, and their input tensor shapes correlate directly with compile time. Larger graphs on larger tensors take longer to compile. title: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide
abstract: Most fine-tuning teaches a model to produce a better answer to a single prompt. Agentic tasks are different. An agent that files an expense report or triages a support ticket takes a sequence of actions, and each step depends on what came before. There’s rarely one correct sequence to imitate, and the only reliable feedback is whether the whole sequence succeeded. Supervised fine-tuning has no labels for that, and single-turn reinforcement learning cannot credit a decision made three steps before the outcome. Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI trains models on exactly that signal. SageMaker AI sends prompts to an agent you host on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, or on your own infrastructure, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), or AWS Fargate, through an AWS Lambda forwarder . The example here uses AgentCore. The agent calls the policy model being trained, acts in your environment over as many turns as the task needs, and reports one reward when the episode ends. You don’t specify the right trajectory, only how to score the result. This post uses Wordle , a game in which a player has six tries to guess a hidden five-letter word, as the example. After each guess, every letter turns green if it is in the right position, yellow if it’s in the word but in a different position, and gray if it isn’t in the word. The game suits MTRL because the rules are few, each guess depends on the feedback from the last, and the outcome is scored objectively. Wordle is a teaching example, and frontier models already play it well. In practice, you would use MTRL to make a small, low-cost model good at a multi-step task specific to your business, such as an internal workflow that public models were never trained on. The same pipeline applies to that setting. In our run, MTRL took gpt-oss-20b from a 61 to an 84 percent solve rate on held-out words at its default reasoning effort, and from 15 to 69 percent at the low effort it trained at, for about $339 in training tokens. In this post, we walk through the pipeline end-to-end: deploying the agent and reward to AgentCore, preparing the dataset, training, monitoring in MLflow, and evaluating at serving settings. We also share the reward-design mistakes and training failures we hit. Your datasets, agent, and trained model stay in your AWS account and are not used to train the base models . All code is in the accompanying aws-samples repository . Solution overview The system has two halves. SageMaker AI owns the training job and the policy model. AgentCore hosts the agent, the Wordle environment, and the reward function. The following diagram shows how they connect. Figure 1: MTRL on SageMaker AI, where the training job invokes the AgentCore-hosted agent once per rollout to sample the policy model, play the game, and report a reward For every rollout, the MTRL service invokes the AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with one training row, which holds one secret word. A Strands agent in the runtime calls the policy model through the SageMaker Job Runtime’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The model plays up to six guesses through one tool, guess_word , and after each guess the environment returns per-letter feedback and a summary of what is known. When the game ends, the agent returns one reward. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) uses the spread of rewards across several rollouts of the same word to update a Low-Rank Adaptation ( LoRA ) adapter on the policy model. Three design points matter for what follows: The agent and reward live in one place. A single Python file deployed to AgentCore holds the environment, the tool, and the scoring function. The dataset carries only the secret word. The word lists bundled with the agent are built from the open-source SCOWL word lists and are used only for scoring. The reward is outcome-dominant. title: Orchestrating SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling with AWS CDK
abstract: Updating the Amazon Sagemaker AI real-time endpoint configuration (changing the instance type, instance count, or environment variables) causes deployments through AWS CloudFormation or the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to fail. SageMaker AI requires you to deregister the scalable target before updating the endpoint, but when you deregister it, CloudFormation can’t track the AWS Application Auto Scaling resources. In this post, we show you how to use a reusable CDK construct with AWS CloudFormation custom resources to orchestrate deregister and register auto scaling automatically during endpoint updates. You can update your endpoint configuration and auto scaling parameters in a single deployment without manual intervention. Why this problem occurs When you deploy a SageMaker AI endpoint with native CloudFormation auto scaling resources, then change the endpoint configuration and redeploy, several failure modes emerge. The specific failure depends on what you change and how you work around the issue. Changing the endpoint configuration with auto scaling registered CloudFormation tries to update the endpoint while the scalable target is still registered. SageMaker AI rejects the update with the following error: The variant(s) "[AllTraffic]" must be deregistered as scalable targets with Application Auto Scaling before they can be removed or have their instance type updated. SageMaker AI blocks the endpoint update before CloudFormation reaches the auto scaling resources. Manually deregistering auto scaling, then changing only the endpoint configuration If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and redeploy with only an endpoint configuration change, the deployment succeeds. However, CloudFormation doesn’t register auto scaling even though it is in the CloudFormation template. Because the auto scaling parameters in the CloudFormation template haven’t changed, CloudFormation doesn’t register the scalable target or re-apply the scaling policy. The endpoint is now running without auto scaling, and there is no error to indicate anything went wrong. Manually deregistering auto scaling, then changing auto scaling parameters If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS CLI and redeploy with auto scaling parameter changes, CloudFormation tries to update the ScalableTarget resource that no longer exists: Resource of type 'AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget' with identifier 'endpoint/<name>/variant/AllTraffic|sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount|sagemaker' was not found. This failure is notable because the rollback also fails (UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED), leaving the stack in a broken state that requires manual intervention in the CloudFormation console to recover. Solution overview You can use this CDK construct to replace the native AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget and AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalingPolicy CloudFormation resources with three custom resources. These custom resources deregister and register auto scaling around the endpoint update with explicit dependency ordering, enforced by node.add_dependency calls in CDK. The full sequence is: Deregister (custom resource): Removes the scalable target before the endpoint update begins. On first deploy, no scalable target exists yet, so the handler handles the error gracefully and continues. Endpoint update (CDK-managed): CDK updates the endpoint resource normally, swapping to the new endpoint configuration. Register Scalable Target (custom resource): Waits for the endpoint to reach InService status, then registers the scalable target. Attach Scaling Policy (custom resource): Waits for the scalable target to be queryable, then applies the target tracking policy. title: Visualize points and routes with GeoJSON in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps
abstract: With Amazon Quick Sight layer maps, you can now plot points and routes, like store locations across a city or flights leaving an airport. Geospatial maps help businesses spot patterns that are tied to location, like how a region is performing or where customers are concentrated. Amazon Quick Sight supports this with multiple map types, including point maps, filled maps, and layer maps. When layer maps first launched , you could upload a GeoJSON file to draw custom shape layers, such as sales territories or districts, and join those shapes to a dataset. That handled regions and boundaries well, but it didn’t cover the individual locations inside them or the routes running between them. Layer maps now support two more geometry types from the same GeoJSON workflow: Point and LineString . Points mark specific locations, such as individual store or facility sites. A LineString traces the route between locations, like a delivery path or a flight between airports. Amazon Quick Sight , the business intelligence (BI) capability of Amazon Quick , is a unified BI service. It delivers modern interactive dashboards, natural language querying, pixel-perfect reports, machine learning (ML) insights, and embedded analytics at scale. Amazon Quick brings together AI agents for business insights, research, and automation in one integrated experience, helping you work smarter and faster while maintaining security and access policies. In this post, we walk through the dataset and GeoJSON structure that layer maps require. We also explain how points and lines work in a layer map visual and when to choose each. Finally, we cover advanced techniques for controlling the viewport, layering geometries, and updating GeoJSON files programmatically. Dataset structure considerations A layer map gets its shapes from a GeoJSON file and its metrics from a Quick Sight dataset, and a shared key joins the two. How you structure each one determines what the map can show. This section covers what you need before you start and how a GeoJSON file is organized. Prerequisites The following are the prerequisites that you need before creating a layer map in Quick Sight: A GeoJSON file describing your geometry. A Quick Sight dataset holding the metrics and dimensions. A join key shared between the Quick Sight dataset and the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON file must be saved in .geojson format, with a maximum supported file size of 100 MB. Structure of the GeoJSON file GeoJSON is a JSON-based format for describing geographic features such as points and lines. { "type": "FeatureCollection", "features": [{ "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [88.4, 22.6] }, "properties": { "prop0": "value0" } }, { "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "LineString", "coordinates": [ [88.2, 22.4], [88.9, 23.1], [89.5, 22.8], [90.1, 23.6] ] }, "properties": { "prop0": "value0" } }] } The structure of the file is as follows: FeatureCollection is the whole file. It has a type of FeatureCollection and a features array. Feature is a single map element. It carries a geometry (the shape) and a properties object, which holds the join key. geometry has a type (Point, LineString, or Polygon) and its coordinates . The coordinates hold a single [longitude, latitude] position for a Point , and an ordered list of positions for a LineString . Configuring the Quick Sight dataset and its GeoJSON In Quick Sight, when you configure a layer in a layer map visual, there are two primary settings to consider. The first is the Geometry type to visualize , which sets which geometry from the GeoJSON file renders: Points, Lines, or Polygons. A layer renders one geometry type at a time, so when a file mixes types like the preceding example, only Features of the selected type appear on the map. title: How Bayer Crop Science built an agentic decision engine on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with AWS Unified Operations
abstract: Plant breeding decisions depend on data that spans genomics, field trials, imagery, environmental conditions, and model outputs. Bayer Crop Science runs hundreds of machine learning (ML) model configurations against this data across crops, regions, and teams, and each run needs to be repeatable and governed. To meet that requirement, Bayer built the Connected Decision Engine (CDE), a system for deploying, orchestrating, monitoring, and reusing ML workflows. CDE gives breeders, analysts, researchers, data scientists, and data engineers a consistent way to run analytics while preserving execution history and operational controls. As adoption grew, the bottleneck moved from running workflows to understanding them. Explaining a result meant piecing together context from APIs, documentation, metadata stores, dashboards, and logs. A user who wanted to know why a workflow failed, what a model did, or where a result came from still had to know which system to inspect. To close that gap, Bayer built the Agentic Decision Engine (ADE), a multi-agent, natural language interface over CDE. A supervisor agent routes each question to a specialist agent, the specialist retrieves context from the relevant system, and the user receives an answer without navigating the operational stack. In its first phase, ADE resolves about 80 percent of user questions without an engineer in the loop. ADE runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , an AWS service to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore let the team focus on agent behavior instead of building and operating its own agent hosting, session isolation, and tool access layer. Three AgentCore capabilities drove that choice: a managed runtime that isolates each user session, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped tool access through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, that keeps authentication and authorization outside agent code, and a framework-agnostic design that let the team bring its own LangGraph orchestration and choice of models. To prepare for launch and to operate ADE afterward, Bayer engaged AWS Unified Operations . The engagement provided a designated Technical Account Manager (TAM) and a generative AI Domain Specialist Engineer (DSE), who worked as an extension of the ADE team from design through production. The TAM, as Bayer’s strategic advisor, brought an established understanding of Bayer’s operating model and business priorities. The DSE brought generative AI domain expertise on AWS. In three technical standups each week, the team reviewed and made design decisions. The DSE built working knowledge of the ADE workload and how the Bayer team operates, so technical guidance reflected both AWS service behavior and Bayer’s context. This post follows that journey: the ADE architecture, five design decisions made during the build, the work to prepare the platform for production, and how it is operated after launch. Architecture overview ADE is organized into four layers: the user experience, agent orchestration, specialist agents, and the tools and data sources those agents call (Figure 1). Users reach ADE through a React web front end, and requests pass through an identity proxy for Microsoft Entra ID before they reach the agents. GitHub Actions builds the agent container images, pushes them to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) , and deploys them to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosts the agents, and because the runtime is framework-agnostic, the team runs its own LangGraph-based orchestration on it directly. The team chose LangGraph for its explicit graph-based control flow and checkpointing for multi-step workflows. LangGraph orchestrates the workflow, with a Supervisor Agent as the entry point that classifies each request, selects a specialist, and combines results when a question spans domains. The data plane is separated by responsibility.

title: How IskayPet unified corporate knowledge with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases
abstract: IskayPet’s office teams had a knowledge challenge. Answers to everyday operational questions, such as a return policy, a veterinary protocol, or an onboarding step, lived in hundreds of Microsoft SharePoint documents spread across four languages and three countries. Finding the right information in large document repositories took a long time. Every new store, country, or procedure made the problem bigger. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is the usual way to solve this. But running RAG in production normally means operating vector databases, embedding pipelines, and ingestion jobs yourself. In this post, we show how IskayPet, a leading pet care company in Iberia, built a corporate knowledge assistant on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases. The assistant answers employee questions across retail operations, veterinary care, people and onboarding, and procurement, in four languages and across three countries, with no RAG infrastructure to manage. The team built the whole solution, from the store-facing frontend to the AWS architecture and deployment, using Kiro with Claude Haiku 4.5. We cover the architecture, the SharePoint integration, the retrieval configuration decisions, and the results in production. About IskayPet IskayPet is a leading pet care company in Iberia. It operates more than 330 stores across Spain, Portugal, and France under the Kiwoko, Tiendanimal, Kivet, Clinicanimal and Animalis brands. With more than 4,500 employees and 7 million customers, IskayPet runs operations that span retail, veterinary clinics, animal care, procurement, and people and onboarding. Each area has its own policies and procedures, in Spanish, Portuguese, French, and English. The challenge Across every business area, IskayPet office staff searched hundreds of SharePoint documents by hand to answer operational questions about procedures, policies, contracts, and onboarding. With operations in three countries and four languages, this took real time, and the answer was often outdated or wrong. There was no reliable way to query corporate knowledge, and the problem grew with every country, area, or document added. IskayPet needed a solution that could do the following: Answer natural-language questions grounded in their own corporate documents. Work across four languages without maintaining separate systems. Route each question to the right body of knowledge (an area, a country) without cross-contamination. Scale to new areas and countries without re-architecting. Cite its sources so employees can trust and verify answers. Reuse their existing SharePoint repositories without a costly migration. Why Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases IskayPet chose Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases for its managed RAG infrastructure, which removed the need to run vector stores, embeddings, or ingestion pipelines. The main reasons were: Managed RAG: Amazon Bedrock handles data ingestion, multimodal parsing, vector storage, embedding generation, and retrieval. IskayPet pays only for what it stores and retrieves. Native SharePoint connector: The connector ingests documents directly from IskayPet’s existing SharePoint environment, which avoided a data migration. With advanced indexing enabled, it also processes content from images embedded in documents. Built-in hybrid search: Combining semantic and keyword (BM25) search at no extra cost recovers exact terms, such as product codes and references, that pure semantic search can miss. Managed reranking: Retrieved passages are reordered by relevance at no additional charge. Document-level access control: The knowledge base can enforce the source system’s own permissions at retrieval time, so a query returns only passages from documents the requesting user is already allowed to read. This lets IskayPet reuse SharePoint permissions instead of rebuilding an authorization model. title: Write your own training loop — without managing GPUs — with Amazon SageMaker training session APIs
abstract: Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) today usually forces a tradeoff between training loop control and operational simplicity. With fully managed services you select a base model, provide data and hyperparameters, and the service owns everything else, which works well when a standard, prepackaged recipe fits your problem. Less managed services give you more control, but you also manage more of the underlying infrastructure and training frameworks. Sometimes a standard recipe isn’t enough: you need a custom loss or data curriculum for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), your own preference optimization, a reinforcement learning (RL) reward function, or an alignment algorithm published last week. As soon as you need to shape the training procedure yourself, you take on that infrastructure work to gain algorithmic freedom. Today, serverless model customization in Amazon SageMaker AI expands with training session APIs, which remove that tradeoff by drawing the abstraction boundary one level lower. Instead of abstracting away the algorithm, they abstract away the compute. Operations like forward_backward() , optim_step() , and sample() become SageMaker API calls that you compose into whatever procedure your technique requires: SFT, preference optimization, RL, or something new. The calls target a live, stateful session, so the model stays loaded on the GPUs across steps, and you drive as many calls as you need against it. The service handles runtime setup, distributed execution, gradient synchronization, fault recovery, tenant isolation, and the operations of running GPUs at scale. You write the training loop, and SageMaker AI runs the infrastructure. Alongside the service, we’re releasing the SageMaker training sessions cookbook , a set of ready-to-run SFT and RL recipes that you can use as blueprints for your own training loops. In this post, we introduce the programming model and the three SDK clients, and show where training session APIs fit among the model training and customization options in SageMaker AI. We then take apart a minimal RL loop on grade-school math problems (GSM8K) to show how the operations fit together and finish with a real-world workload from the cookbook: reinforcement learning on competitive programming problems, where generated code is graded by running it against unit tests. What are SageMaker AI training session APIs? With SageMaker AI training session APIs, you can drive a live, GPU-backed session from your own Python process on your local machine. You call the operations, and SageMaker AI runs them on managed accelerators loaded with your chosen base model plus your Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter. There’s no config file describing the whole job up front and no cluster creation step. You control what happens at each step, interactively, from code, so you can iterate and debug quickly. title: Deploy AI in a HIPAA-eligible environment with Amazon Quick
abstract: Healthcare organizations want the same thing from AI that every other business wants: faster answers, less manual work, and insights that reach decision-makers in time to act on them. However, what makes the healthcare industry different is that the data is uniquely complex, deeply contextual, and strictly regulated. So this post starts with a few definitions to set the foundation for everything that follows. Protected Health Information (PHI) is any information that identifies a person and relates to their health, care, or payment for care, such as a medical note, a claim, or a member ID. When software touches PHI, it falls under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), the federal law that governs how PHI data is accessed, secured, and audited. Agentic AI changes what it means for software to “touch PHI.” A traditional analytics tool reads data and returns a response. An agentic workspace like Amazon Quick might go further. For example, its chat agents work across both unstructured content, such as clinical notes and appeals letters, and structured data, such as claims and member records. Agents might retrieve data from both unstructured and structured sources, call other systems through connectors, and complete multi-step tasks on a user’s behalf. Connectors are pre-built integrations that let Amazon Quick securely read from and take action in your external systems, such as Slack , Microsoft Outlook , Salesforce , Atlassian Jira , and Microsoft SharePoint . You can also add your own custom tools through Model Context Protocol (MCP). Only connectors authorized within your organization are visible. When a chat agent can both read and act on PHI, you need sufficient governance: deterministic guardrails, a behavioral audit trail of what the agent did, and clear accountability for actions taken without a person in the loop. To support that governance, Amazon Quick exposes ACL-aware retrieval, chat and feedback logging, and controls over what each chat agent is allowed to do. Amazon Quick is a HIPAA -eligible service. This eligibility applies across the Amazon Quick web, desktop, and mobile clients, subject to the shared responsibility model and your configuration. This post, however, focuses on the capabilities of the Amazon Quick web version, which you access through your browser. In this post, we start with the foundations: who HIPAA applies to and the difference between HIPAA-eligible and HIPAA-compliant. We then introduce Amazon Quick as a platform and the two data flows for PHI (unstructured and structured). From there, we cover what Amazon Quick provides for regulated environments and what it doesn’t, walk through a fictional health plan (AnyCompany) deployment, and distill the best practices and irreversible decisions you should make up front. We close with a step-by-step implementation guide, a conclusion, and resources for deeper reading. Who does HIPAA apply to? HIPAA reaches further than hospitals and clinics. Under the law, two categories of organizations carry obligations, and most AI projects touch both. Covered entities (CEs) Health plans – Health insurance companies, HMOs, employer-sponsored plans, Medicare, and Medicaid. Healthcare clearinghouses – Organizations that process nonstandard health information into standard electronic formats. Healthcare providers – Doctors, clinics, hospitals, pharmacies, nursing homes, and any provider that transmits health information electronically. Common examples include cloud service providers, IT vendors, billing companies, data analytics firms, claims processors, law firms, and consulting firms. abstract: A customer asks an AI voice agent a question and waits. The agent already has an answer, it’s midway through generating a long, multi-paragraph response, but the customer hears nothing for five seconds. By the time an answer arrives, the customer is frustrated, confused, and no longer paying attention. Text-to-speech integrations create exactly that gap. A one-sentence response might generate in 600 milliseconds, but the full response takes five seconds, and the integration waits for all of it before synthesis starts. This post shows how to close that gap. We stream each sentence to a hosted Kokoro-82M text-to-speech (TTS) model on Amazon SageMaker AI as soon as an agent produces it, so synthesis begins on sentence one instead of the finished response. Getting that audio back to a browser needs its own solution too, so we also cover both transports for doing it and what each costs in practice. Solution overview This solution closes the gap by streaming synthesis alongside generation instead of waiting for it to finish. As the agent produces each sentence, that sentence streams immediately to a hosted Kokoro-82M text-to-speech model, so audio playback can start before the agent finishes speaking its full response. Kokoro-82M holds only 82 million parameters, small enough to run cheaply on a single mid-tier GPU instance. That keeps both latency and inference cost low for a voice agent handling real traffic. Kokoro-82M runs in a custom container on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, on an ml.g5.xlarge GPU instance. The container exposes two routes: POST /invocations , which streams a response for one complete input, and WS /invocations-bidirectional-stream , which keeps one connection open across many messages in both directions. title: Stop guessing auto scaling targets for TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: A traffic spike hits your self-hosted text-to-speech (TTS) endpoint, and requests start queueing. Latency climbs past your service level objective (SLO) right when the most callers are listening. The auto scaling policy behind that endpoint was supposed to prevent this, but the target value it scales on was a guess, and guesses like that fail silently until real traffic proves them wrong. Get that number wrong, and it’s paid for in one of two ways, and neither shows up as an alarm. Guess too conservative, and the fleet runs GPU instances that sit mostly idle. That cost lands on every invoice but never trips an incident report. Guess too aggressive, and the fleet carries a risk nobody sees. Each instance holds more concurrent requests than it can serve inside its latency promise. Nothing looks wrong until a real traffic spike pushes queueing time past the SLO. That happens right when the most callers are listening. That’s the hidden gap. A policy that looks fine on the console can already be failing the people it’s supposed to serve. In this post, we deploy Kokoro-82M , an 82-million-parameter TTS model, as a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) stacks handle the deployment. We replace guesswork with two measurements taken against the live endpoint. Q_max is the highest concurrency one instance sustains before breaching the SLO, and T_total is how long a scale-out takes end to end. We derive the scale-out threshold, scale-in threshold, and both cooldowns from those two numbers by arithmetic. Every number in this post comes from an actual deployment and measurement run of the aws-samples repository referenced in this post. Why default auto scaling metrics don’t work for TTS Most public guidance on Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling targets short synchronous request/response calls, or large language model (LLM) serving, where the natural metric is tokens generated per second. TTS synthesis fits neither pattern: a single request holds a connection open for several seconds with no token-generation loop to attach a metric to. Kokoro-82M is non-autoregressive, a StyleTTS2 derivative with an ISTFTNet decoder, trained adversarially rather than by autoregressive next-token prediction or iterative denoising. It produces a full utterance from one duration-aligned pass. There’s no generation loop to instrument with a per-token metric in the first place. What determines whether a TTS instance is overloaded is simpler than it sounds: how many requests are queued and executing on it right now. The deployed policy scales on ConcurrentRequestsPerModel , a native metric Amazon SageMaker AI publishes itself rather than one this project’s own container code has to emit. Scaling on a metric Amazon SageMaker AI publishes removes an entire class of failure where a custom metric configuration looks correct on paper but nothing is actually publishing to it. ConcurrentRequestsPerModel publishes a Maximum statistic over a 10-second window, a different quantity from the mean in-flight count a benchmarking client measures directly. The tooling accounts for this. At every rung of the concurrency ladder it measures both quantities against the same load and records the ratio between them. It then uses that ratio to convert the client-measured threshold into Amazon CloudWatch units before writing it into the deployable configuration. For the Kokoro-82M run in this post, the measured ratio came out to exactly 1.0 at every rung, so the client-measured and Amazon CloudWatch-reported thresholds match directly. title: How Rescale built an AI triage agent with Strands Agents and AI-DLC
abstract: Every engineering team knows the ritual, and Rescale was no exception. A nightly test suite fails. An on-call engineer pulls the logs, classifies the root cause, and routes it to the right team, only to repeat the process the next morning. At scale, across distributed services and dozens of repositories, this ritual becomes a full-time job hiding inside an on-call rotation. Rescale is the digital engineering platform built for the AI era. R&D and engineering teams across aerospace, automotive, energy, life sciences, semiconductor, and manufacturing use the Rescale platform to accelerate innovation, bringing intelligent HPC, advanced modeling and simulation, agentic digital engineering, and AI physics together on a single platform. Beyond coding, Rescale uses AI across the engineering lifecycle, from planning and design through implementation, testing, review, and operations, while keeping engineers accountable for the result. AI can propose and execute, but people define scope, validate the work, and approve production changes. Engineers can then focus on architecture, product judgment, and the context required to operate complex distributed systems. In this post, we show how Rescale used the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) framework on AWS to build an intelligent triage agent. They went from problem definition to staging deployment in five days, and to production within weeks. The post also covers how Rescale is extending AI-DLC across their engineering organization. The challenge As Rescale’s platform grew, so did the operational overhead of keeping it running. Engineers were spending significant time on a repetitive but critical task: classifying automated end-to-end test failures. Hundreds of test cases run in the suite, and when failures appeared, every alert, bug report, and escalation needed to be classified, prioritized, and routed to the right team. After routing, engineers would need to gather evidence from multiple logging and monitoring systems, along with several source repositories before debugging could even begin. Passing end-to-end tests were required to deploy services to production and thus debugging these system failures was in the critical path to getting new changes to production. In the manual workflow, engineers moved from the test report to logs, historical patterns, and source code to classify failures and identify the likely owning team. Because these integration tests gate weekly production releases, unresolved failures could pull several teams into hours of coordination before a deployment was allowed to proceed. The team had a clear idea of what a solution looked like: an intelligent agent that could classify and route issues automatically. What they were looking for was a structured way to go from that understanding to a working system in production, with enough structure to extend the approach to other use cases afterward. Why Rescale chose AI-DLC Rescale’s triage agent was a well-scoped problem with a tight timeline. The team needed a development approach that could move at that pace without skipping the architectural decisions that would determine whether the system worked in production. The AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) is an open source, AI-centric methodology for software development built around two ideas: AI executes, humans decide: AI generates work plans, writes code, and proposes architecture, but it surfaces decision points and asks clarifying questions rather than guessing. Humans validate and steer at each step. Team sessions replace async handoffs: Instead of one person building alone and requesting review later, AI-DLC uses focused group sessions: Mob Elaboration (defining requirements together) and Mob Construction (building together while AI handles implementation). title: Securing Quick access from corporate networks with AWS PrivateLink
abstract: When enterprise data sits behind a corporate firewall or in a private on-premises data center, there’s no direct network path from AWS, even though the AI agents and dashboards in Amazon Quick can query virtually any data source. Administrators must make sure their sensitive enterprise data isn’t exposed to the public internet while being accessible for AI-driven insights and actions. For many enterprises, routing traffic over the public internet introduces unacceptable risk. Regulatory frameworks such as HIPAA, FedRAMP, and PCI-DSS often mandate that sensitive data remain within controlled network boundaries. Even where compliance isn’t the primary driver, exposing internal data paths increases the attack surface, complicates audit trails and introduces variable latency that can degrade the user experience. This walkthrough shows you how to connect on-premises data sources to Amazon Quick privately, without traffic traversing the public internet. It assumes you already have AWS Direct Connect or an AWS Site-to-Site VPN linking your on-premises environment to your virtual private cloud (VPC). From that foundation, we configure VPC endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink so that Quick can reach your private resources over the AWS backbone, then layer security groups and VPC endpoint policies for defense in depth. By the end, you will have a network architecture that keeps traffic between Quick and your on-premises data sources off the public internet, reducing the attack surface, providing consistent low-latency connectivity, and giving you a clear audit trail for compliance. Amazon Quick and establishing private network connectivity Amazon Quick is an AI-powered workspace that brings search, analytics, research, and automation into a single conversational experience. Understanding which components reach your private network, and how, determines the architecture in the sections that follow. Data access in Amazon Quick falls into two paths. User-facing traffic covers anyone opening the Quick console, interacting with a dashboard, making an API call, or using Quick Desktop. All this routes through VPC endpoints (see VPC endpoints for user and API access), keeping user sessions off the public internet. Data-fetching traffic is when Quick itself reaches into your network to pull data. This is handled by VPC connections (see VPC connections for data source access), and it’s where most of the architectural decisions lie. Any workflow that calls an internal API routes through this path. Quick Agents underpin all conversational interactions and can invoke action connectors directly. title: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them
abstract: Building a multi-agent system is now pretty straightforward. Taking it to production is where the real challenges begin. Thanks to open source frameworks and cloud services, you can set up an agent in a matter of days. A few tool calls, a few lines of prompt, and you have something that looks impressive. But the moment teams try to move beyond a pilot and into real business applications, they hit a familiar wall. If you’ve ever tried to put an agent into production, these frustrations will sound familiar: Why doesn’t the agent follow our business logic, skip validation steps, or catch edge cases? You tweak the prompt, add more examples, swap out the model. The same problems keep coming back. That’s because agents don’t follow a fixed sequence of instructions. They make their own judgments based on context. Instructions alone aren’t enough. You need to design how the agent thinks, when it verifies, and what it does when things go wrong. This is exactly why it’s become critical to go beyond prompt engineering alone and design the agent’s entire cognitive architecture and execution flow. To tackle these challenges head-on, the AWS Solutions Architecture team built Deep Insight , a production-grade multi-agent system. In this post series, we share what the team learned firsthand while building Deep Insight across three posts. We will walk through how we applied Context Engineering techniques proposed by Anthropic (multi-agent architecture, structured note-taking, human-in-the-loop, and more) in a real production environment. We also cover the trade-offs we encountered along the way (with code) and the operational insights we gained from deploying and running this agent on AWS. Part 2: Beyond the context window: Context Engineering techniques and how Deep Insight applied them. Part 3: Harness engineering in practice: moving Deep Insight from dev to production. This is Part 1 of a three-part series. It defines the five core challenges any production multi-agent system must solve and shows how each layer of the stack addresses them, from Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , Application Load Balancer , and AWS Fargate . Parts 2 and 3 cover Context Engineering and production deployment. Introducing Deep Insight Deep Insight is a multi-agent system that turns complex data analysis into automated insights. Given a CSV file and a natural-language prompt, a hierarchy of specialized agents (Coordinator, Planner, Supervisor, Coder, Validator, Reporter, and Tracker) collaborates on the analysis. Together they load the data, run analyses, generate charts, validate calculations, and produce a professional report (.docx) with citations. We will explore the architecture in detail later. First, let’s see it in action. For the demo, we feed advertising data from a fictional food company, Yummy Food ( yummy-food-market.csv ) with a column definitions file ( column_definitions.json ), and provide the prompt: Analyze this from a sales and marketing perspective, generate charts and insights, and produce a .docx report. Deep Insight generates an analysis plan, presents it to the user for approval, and, once approved, executes the analysis. abstract: By Roberto Perez Alcolea , Java Platform Team Quasar connects a proposed API change with observed references in consumer repositories, giving the producer evidence for a release decision At Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed. The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it. Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves. Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. The producer still cannot answer the questions that determine what to do next: Does any consumer still call this method? Are consumers concentrated on one version or spread across several generations? Does another library implement or wrap the API, multiplying its impact? Is direct coordination sufficient, or does this require a deprecation and migration campaign? At small scale, producers can ask nearby teams or search a handful of repositories. Across many repositories, it is harder to find every caller of a method and the library version each one uses. Those answers are scattered across consumer codebases and builds. Without that evidence, a producer may release a breaking change and discover the impact through consumer failures, or preserve an old API indefinitely because the risk is unknown. Libraries need to evolve, and their producers need evidence that helps them do so intentionally. We built Quasar to index symbol definitions and references across Netflix repositories. For library producers, that shared index helps answer two questions: What changed in the library’s public API? Which repositories use the exact symbols that changed? The first identifies a potentially incompatible change. The second estimates its observed blast radius. Together, they turn a generic compatibility warning into evidence a producer can act on before merging or releasing. From API Changes to Consumer Impact Existing techniques each see a different part of the problem. Binary and source compatibility tools identify contract changes, but cannot tell who uses the changed API. Dependency graphs show declared reach, but cannot prove that code calls a particular method. Text search may miss overloads, inheritance, or the artifact version behind a call. Consumer builds provide strong validation, but running them across the fleet is expensive. Quasar builds on SCIP , an open interchange format for semantic code intelligence. Language-specific indexers encode definitions, references, and relationships using stable symbol identifiers. Quasar retains API definitions for library versions and commits alongside references from consumer repositories. That shared identity lets it connect an API change in one repository to exact usages elsewhere, even when those repositories were indexed independently. On each enrolled CI build, language-specific indexers submit SCIP indexes to Quasar’s ingestion service. It writes API definitions and consumer references as Parquet in Amazon S3, retaining the symbol identity, dependency version, and source location needed to investigate a change. During pull-request review, Quasar compares indexed base and head definitions and counts direct consumer references with Amazon Athena. Quasar exposes those findings

title: Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform
abstract: Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick Parker You click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years. For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run. This post is about them, and about single-tenant Titus, a mode that gives a task its own virtual machine while keeping everything else about Titus the same: the API, the deployment path, and the managed experience where the Compute/Platform team, not the application team, owns the host. We will walk through why shared-kernel isolation runs out of road for certain workloads, how we measure isolation rather than asserting it, the options we weighed (microVMs, gVisor, EC2, and more shared-kernel tuning) and why a dedicated VM inside Titus won, how the mode is built on the Titus federation layer and autoscaling, and what we have seen along three axes: isolation, fleet efficiency, and the operational cost of keeping the fleet patched. The cost of good neighbors Multi-tenancy is a tradeoff. Packing many containers onto a large bare-metal instance keeps utilization high, but it also means those containers share a single Linux kernel and the underlying hardware. Titus isolates them with the tools the kernel provides: cgroups cap CPU, memory, and disk; namespaces give each container its own view of the system; seccomp and AppArmor restrict the system calls a container can make; the Completely Fair Scheduler divides CPU time; the iocost controller meters disk IO; and traffic shaping meters each container’s slice of the network. Each container also gets its own identity, IAM role, and security groups, so tenants are isolated for security and resource management. These mechanisms provide isolation for what the kernel can partition. They cannot fully partition what is shared in hardware. A group of cores shares a last-level cache and a path to memory, so a container that suddenly pulls a lot of data from RAM evicts a neighbor’s cache lines and slows it down, even when both stay inside their CPU limits. There is no cgroup for memory bandwidth or cache residency, as there is for CPU shares. The interference is real, it is hardware, and it does not show up as either container exceeding its quota. A noisy neighbor and a co-located app each stay within their cgroup CPU and memory limits, but both draw on a shared last-level cache and memory bandwidth that lack cgroup fences. The noisy neighbor takes most of it, so the co-located app stalls and its tail latency rises even though no one exceeded a quota. We have written about this before. Predictive CPU isolation of containers at Netflix moved some placement decisions out of the kernel and into a service that forecasts each container’s CPU demand and re-pins containers to cores to reduce cache interference, formulated as a combinatorial optimization solved every minute. Noisy Neighbor Detection with eBPF instruments the kernel scheduler to surface per-container run-queue latency, so we can see a victim being starved in close to real time. Owners, Not Renters: Raffi Krikorian on Open Source AI
abstract: Created by Claude with light editing by Tim O’Reilly Raffi Krikorian, Mozilla’s CTO, joined Tim O’Reilly at our recent AI Codecon to talk about open source AI. Mozilla, of course, is the nonprofit that helped to define the open source revolution back in the late 1990s. Though its Firefox web browser was superseded as the market leader by Google Chrome, it played an essential role, along with Apache and the World Wide Web Consortium, in establishing the open standards of the web and keeping it from being dominated and enclosed by Microsoft, the dominant tech platform of that time. Now, Mozilla is one of the leading voices working to build an open, standards-based AI ecosystem. Tim has long appreciated Raffi’s thoughtful, human-centered approach to technology. Raffi writes a newsletter called Owners Not Renters , whose message can be summed up by his statement that he doesn’t want a future with seven AGIs. He wants one with seven billion. He wants each of us to have an AI that we can trust with our secrets and that will look out for our interests, not an AI that’s optimized for the business model of its creators. In the early days of the web, we called the browser a user agent for a reason, Raffi said. It was on your side. It let you render pages however you wanted, managed your privacy and your cookies, and did its best to protect you from those who wanted to take advantage of web users. We need the same thing in the age of AI. Raffi cited a paper in which researchers tested whether AI assistants could be trained to favor a company’s commercial interests over user welfare. In simulated flight-booking requests, 18 of 23 models recommended a more expensive sponsored option over a cheaper one more than half the time. It’s a hypothetical choice that we’ve seen play out time and time again, in industry after industry. Open source AI is a big part of what it will take to get to Raffi’s vision. But sovereign AI loyal to each individual needs more than open source models alone. Raffi’s list of what has to be built around the model starts with memory, a place where your private data can live. It includes tool calling, so an agent can make a purchase or book a doctor’s appointment for you, the runtime environment where all of that runs, and the rules for how his agent talks to those working on behalf of others. It needs a harness. “That’s where evaluations happen. Guardrails happen, execution loops happen, tool calling happens, memory,” he explained. “All of that stuff is an opportunity, in my mind, of things that open source developers can be building.” People hear the word “harness” and conclude that we need an open source version of whatever the proprietary labs are building. Tim asked Raffi whether a user-centered harness might do different things than those offered by the big labs. He agreed. The whole point of open source is for people to “scratch their own itch.” The ability to innovate without permission is the heart of the open source promise. As a result, Mozilla wants to build a starting point. It aims to help the community define what an open memory protocol, a storage protocol, or authenticated tool calling with the right guardrails ought to look like. As Raffi noted, “Once we could define what those open standards look like, then a whole plethora of people can start playing and be interoperable. It’s basically. . .the internet all over again. We can build trillions of dollars of market cap on top of open protocols.” Ease of use is still lacking, though. Mozilla’s 2026 State of Open Source AI report says open models are now within about 3% of the frontier, yet they don’t make it into production at the same rate as closed models. When Tim asked why, Raffi explained that open source is easy to release but hard to deploy. Developers still have to figure out hosting, provisioning, guardrails, and memory. title: The Agentic Software Factory Hierarchy of Needs
abstract: The following article originally appeared on the Vanishing Gradients Substack and is being republished here with the authors’ permission. Stripe’s Minions turn engineering requests into candidate pull requests. Ramp’s Inspect puts coding agents to work in the background, with tools to check their changes. Warp Factories takes work from tickets and chat through agents, checks, and human review. Agentic software factories are here. Are you sick and tired of babysitting Codex, Claude Code, or OpenClaw? Do you have agents that can build features, but still leave you responsible for remembering where they stopped, explaining how each feature fits the project and deciding what happens next? You make progress in each conversation, then development waits for you to return. It doesn’t have to be this way. A software factory lets you delegate more of that process! You agree on an outcome, give the system the context and authority it needs, and let it work while you do something else. When you return, there should be a result you can inspect, with evidence of what was checked, or a specific reason the work could not continue. Your next conversation can then focus on the result and the decisions that remain. As we’ll show you, your first software factory doesn’t need to be that complex at all: It can begin with a single agent and an automation. What makes it a factory The defining combination is autonomous and asynchronous execution . Autonomous: The agent chooses and carries out steps towards an agreed goal. It can inspect what happened, adjust its approach and continue within its authority. Asynchronous: That work can proceed without your ongoing attention. You can leave and return to its result. A scheduled job can run without you. A coding agent can choose and revise an approach during an interactive session. A factory combines those capabilities, with enough context, tools and feedback to carry out the delegated work. Software factories have been hypothesized for decades. Now that we have agents, we’re actually able to operate them. The principles apply to software work traditionally carried out by teams of humans, from bespoke tools for teams and individuals to large and complex software systems. To illustrate these principles, we’ll use an invoice tracker throughout this article, an application we’ve needed for our own businesses. The same approach applies to research tools, publishing systems, and software for teams. Suppose you run a small business and want an invoice tracker that fits how you work. Build an app that creates invoices from my template and tracks which are unpaid, paid, or overdue. Keep it local for now. Preserve the records when it restarts, and show me checks that the totals and payment statuses are correct. You can agree on this brief with the agent, leave it to work while you do something else, and return to the app and evidence of what was checked. If a check fails, it can investigate and adjust within its agreed scope. If it encounters a product decision it cannot make, it should bring that question back to you. You might imagine a clean separation: The factory builds the invoice tracker, then the finished app does its job. That’s one way to run it. But agents can also help operate the software they build, and that combination is useful. The tracker can store invoices and calculate outstanding balances. An agent can use those records alongside customer correspondence to prepare follow-ups: One customer has promised to pay on Friday; another is disputing a charge. You don’t need to turn every situation into a new software feature before the agent can help. You give it the relevant context, authority, and a way to check its work. title: The Latest Anthropic Claude Models Contain AI Text Watermarks: What Does This Mean for You?
abstract: If you’re an instructor for the O’Reilly live training platform, you’ve got to be prepared for the unexpected. As a developer I think we all can understand the situation when a demo (you know, the one that you’ve tested a thousand times on your machine) easily decides on its own to go wrong while being demonstrated to a live audience. We’ve all been there. And of course, the biggest variable in the equation is the live Q&A portion of any course, because we actively encourage course participants to ask any question that’s on their mind. Shortly after Anthropic announced that they were going to include AI watermarking in all text-based outputs from their latest models, I was flooded with questions during a Q&A session in a completely unrelated course about Claude Agents. Nearly everyone who posted a question in the Q&A box wanted to know more about how AI watermarking worked, and how it would affect them. In light of that interest, I am taking this opportunity to help explain what watermarking means for you. What did Anthropic officially announce? I don’t want to put words in anyone’s mouth, so I’ll just quote Anthropic verbatim from its announcement in August 2026 : Future Claude models will generate text that contains a watermark. This is a way of determining the likelihood that Claude was involved in writing the text, and we, along with several other major AI providers, are implementing this change to comply with the EU AI Act. Here’s another quote from the same announcement: Watermarking won’t be specific to Claude. As of August 2, the EU requires AI providers serving its market to mark AI-generated content. Other major model developers have signed the same Code of Practice and will be implementing their own watermarks. The list of Claude models (at the time of this writing) that include AI text watermarks in all generated outputs are: Claude Mythos 5.1 Claude Fable 5.1 Claude Fable 5 Claude Opus 5.5 Claude Opus 5 Claude Opus 4.8 Claude Sonnet 5.5 Claude Sonnet 5 Claude Haiku 5.5 It won’t matter if you use Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or the API, because all of Claude’s outputs will contain the AI watermark. As a result, any code, email, blog, article, newsletter, or white paper that you write using Claude will contain a watermark, and anyone who has an AI watermark detector can easily determine if that content was AI generated. What’s the difference between cryptography and steganography? Now let’s talk about two related terms that apply to what we’re dealing with when it comes to the AI watermarks: cryptography and steganography. Cryptography is something you encounter every day when you visit a website that uses HTTPS instead of HTTP. Your web browser automatically handles the encrypting and the decrypting for you, but what it simply does is make the content of anything that you send or receive unintelligible unless you have the key to decrypt the message. As a result, you can (for example) securely type in your credit card to sign up for an O’Reilly subscription, because we (like every other major website on the internet) use HTTPS on our website to ensure that no outsider can obtain your credit card information. Therefore, if an unscrupulous person intercepts something you send over an HTTPS connection, the contents will be encrypted and meaningless. Steganography is completely different, and it’s what the Claude AI watermarking technology uses. Steganography is about hiding something in the right place for someone who knows where to look for it. title: Building Reasoning Models from the Ground Up: A Full Video Course
abstract: I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs . Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode. For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work. Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content). We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite). I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along! How LLMs, reasoning models, and agents relate and fit together As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos. A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well. A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools. Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article. In this analogy depicted in the figure above, the model is the engine, and the agent harness adds the machinery that lets us use it for various things (as an upgrade from a simple chatbot interface). An agent can use either a conventional LLM or a reasoning model, but reasoning models are the more typical choice as they are more capable. (As mentioned above, most current-gen LLMs are reasoning models with variable reasoning effort settings.) So, the bottom line is that reasoning models, as the “engine,” remain an important part of understanding modern LLM agents. The resources accompanying these topics shown above are: The Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book and videos The Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book (and videos below) The Components of a Coding Agent article on Substack The videos below focus on developing the reasoning model that can power such a system. Scope and prerequisites The reasoning-from-scratch videos focus on a small pre-trained Qwen3 model, where we implement the reasoning methods ourselves in Python and PyTorch. Starting with a pre-trained model lets us focus on the interesting part: evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. Regarding the prerequisites, I recommend being comfortable with Python and PyTorch. title: In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
abstract: Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything , the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes. I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood , and the Hulu series The Dropout , starring Amanda Seyfried. Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything . In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19. She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood. Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014. Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old. Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work. Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead. MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015 . Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016. That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong. In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. She began serving her sentence in May 2023. It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children. I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film. As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer , there are plenty of super close-ups. I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people.
